exact_quote: Geographic Variation Monotypic; no geographic variation. Subspecies Monotypic. Related Species Described as Hirundo leucopyga by Meyen in 1834. The species name used for the [the bird] has oscillated between leucopyga (e.g., Hellmayr 1932, Hellmayr 1935, Peters 1960, Meyer de Schauensee 1966, Ridgely and Tudor 1989, Turner and Rose 1989, Fjeldså and Krabbe 1990) and meyeni (e.g., Brooke 1974, Jaramillo 2003, Schulenberg et al. 2007), depending upon whether the name leucopyga is considered to be preoccupied by another, earlier use of this name. Although meyeni currently is the most commonly used name, Mlíkovský and Frahnert (2009) argue that the original name leucopgya is valid and should be resurrected for this species.The species of the current genus [the bird] formerly (e.g. Ridgway 1904) were distributed among four different genera; the [the bird], meyeni, previously was included in the genus Iridoprocne, which also included the species bicolor (Tree Swallow), albilinea (Mangrove Swallow), leucorrhoa (White-rumped Swallow), albiventer (White-winged Swallow), and stolzmanni (Tumbes Swallow). Later Brooke (1974) proposed two subgenera for [the bird] - Leucochelidon and [the bird] - and placed meyeni in the subgenus Leucochelidon, along with albilinea (and thus, stolzmanni), leucorrhoa, and albiventer.Using mitochondrial DNA sequence data, Whittingham et al. (2002) confirmed the monophyly of [the bird]. Whittingham et al. (2002) also recovered two clades within [the bird], which are consistent with the two subgenera proposed by Brooke. Therefore, the [the bird] belongs to a clade that primarily is made up of South American species. Within this clade, meyeni is the sister species to leucorrhoa; those two species in turn are sister to stolzmanni, albiventer, and albilinea.

Option E is correct as the text mentions that species of the current genus [the bird] were formerly distributed among four different genera, including Iridoprocne.

question: Based on the provided text, which of the following statements correctly describe morphological features that distinguish Phylloscopus rotiensis from other leaf warbler species?

exact_quote: The combination of yellow-orange mandible, white inner vanes to the outermost rectrices, presence and colour of the median crown stripe, and yellow throat, distingishes [the bird] from all of the geographically adjacent [the bird] species, as follows. Compared to Mountain Leaf Warbler (P. trivirgatus), the present species has duller olive upperparts, duller yellow on the body, a duller yellow supercilium and median crown stripe, and a yellow-orange mandible (mostly dark in Mountain Leaf Warbler). The latter also lacks a wingbar and white in the outer tail feathers. Versus Timor Leaf Warbler (P. presbytes), [the bird] has a much stronger median crown stripe, with overall duller coloration, paler yellow underparts, supercilium and ear-coverts, and duller olive-brown upperparts. Like Mountain Leaf Warbler, Timor Leaf Warbler also has a mostly dark mandible. Flores Leaf Warbler (P. presbytes floresianus) has a much less prominent median crown stripe than the present species, as well as richer olive-brown upperparts, and richer orange-yellow underparts. The mandible of Flores Leaf Warbler is dark-tipped. Sulawesi Leaf Warbler (P. sarasinorum) in South Sulawesi has much paler yellow-washed underparts, whereas the upperparts are richer olive-brown, but its supercilium and median crown stripe are both paler, and the mandible is mainly dark. P. sarasinorum nesophilus, over the rest of Sulawesi, has an olive-yellow breast and vent, darker brownish-olive upperparts, a faint or no median crown stripe, paler supercilium, mostly dark mandible, and no white inner vanes to the outermost tail feathers. In the North Moluccas, Island Leaf Warbler (P. maforensis waterstradti) wholly lacks a median crown stripe, and the supercilium and throat are white (not yellow), while the tail feathers are wholly olive-brown (lacking any white vanes), the upperparts are brighter olive-green, the underparts deeper yellow, and the mandible is mostly dark. On Buru, Island Leaf Warbler (P. maforensis everetti) also lacks any median crown stripe, and the supercilium and throat are white and pale gray, respectively (not yellow), the underparts are bright sulphur-yellow, and again the mandible is mostly dark. On Seram, Island Leaf Warbler (P. maforensis ceramensis) has an olive-colored (not yellow) median crown stripe, a whitish supercilium and throat, brighter yellow underparts, no white inner vanes to the outermost rectrices, and a mostly dark mandible.
provenance.reasoning_chain: Option A is correct because the text states that [the bird] has a yellow-orange mandible, while Timor Leaf Warbler has a mostly dark mandible. Option B is correct because [the bird] has white inner vanes to the outermost rectrices, and Island Leaf Warbler (P. maforensis ceramensis) lacks these white inner vanes. Option C is correct because [the bird] has a more prominent median crown stripe than Flores Leaf Warbler. Option D is incorrect because the text says [the bird] has a bill that is 'c. 15% longer than that of Timor Leaf Warbler,' not shorter. Option E is incorrect because the text mentions that Mountain Leaf Warbler 'lacks a wingbar,' implying [the bird] does have one (supported by the 'Plumages' section describing a wingbar), so this statement misattributes the feature.

options.B: It has white inner vanes to the outermost rectrices, which are absent in Island Leaf Warbler (P. maforensis ceramensis).
options.C: It has a median crown stripe that is more prominent than in Flores Leaf Warbler (P. presbytes floresianus).
options.D: It has a shorter bill compared to Timor Leaf Warbler (P. presbytes), being about 15% shorter.

Nest a fairly large, shallow, untidy cup built from thin twigs, rootlets, grass and plant fibres, in Peninsular Malaysia lengths of fine creeper stalks and rhizomes of a small climbing fern (Drymoglossum piloselloides) often incorporated as binding and camouflage; nests found 1·5–6 m above ground, usually in branch fork of small tree along stream (sometimes overhanging water) or standing out from other vegetation in clearing or second growth, less often in low orchard or plantation tree, e.g. mango (Mangifera) or rubber (Hevea). question: Based on the provided text, which of the following descriptions are correct regarding the breeding behavior and nesting of Hypsipetes olivaceus?

exact_quote: Nesting recorded Nov–Feb; probably single-brooded. Monogamous. Co-operative breeding possible based on third bird feeding young at one nest. Traditional territory may be reclaimed from year to year, vigorously defended by both partners; male frequently gives aerial display to mate, using rapid, exaggerated wingbeats, with tail raised and slightly fanned, while giving a series of “chuckle” notes with head thrown back. Nest built by female (one nest only), a coarse cup made of twigs, coarse grass, leaves, roots(?), moss and lichens, lined with finer material, external diameter 13–23 cm, placed 2–9 m above ground on horizontal branch in low bush or tree, often Japanese red cedar (Cryptomeria japonica) where available; territory c. 1 ha around nest. Clutch 3 eggs, in one case completed in 4 days (first and second eggs laid 2 days apart); if clutch lost, repeat laid 8–9 days later in new nest; incubation, by presumed female only, 15–16 days; chicks brooded by presumed female only, fed by both parents, once also by third individual (probably immature?), nestling period 3 weeks; family-members may remain together once young feeding independently. Success poor; fledged broods of one, less often two, juveniles rarely seen; signs of failure consistent with attacks by introduced black rats (Rattus rattus) or crab-eating macaques (Macaca fascicularis).
provenance.reasoning_chain: Option A is correct as the text states 'Nesting recorded Nov–Feb; probably single-brooded.' Option C is incorrect as the text indicates 'Clutch 3 eggs, in one case completed in 4 days (first and second eggs laid 2 days apart)', not 2 eggs laid 1 day apart.

question: Based on the provided monograph, which of the following statements accurately describe the conservation status and threats faced by Rukia longirostra?

exact_quote: Conservation status on Birdlife NT Near Threatened Not globally threatened. Currently considered Near-threatened. Restricted-range species: present in East Caroline Islands EBA. question: Based on its taxonomic history as described in the text, which of the following statements are correct regarding Laticilla cinerascens?

exact_quote: First described as Eurycercus cinerascens in 1874, based on the type from Dhubri, Assam (formerly "Lower Bengal"). Eventually split from Rufous-vented Grass Babbler on the basis of its thinner bill, shorter tail, generally weaker streaking on the upperparts, overall grayer color, and grayish (versus rufous) undertail coverts, as well as differences in egg color. Following this, [the bird] was moved back to the genus [the bird] and removed from the warbler family Sylviidae, together with Rufous-vented Grass Babbler, after phylogenetic studies revealed the genus to belong in the [the bird]. The newly described subspecies nepalicola (nipalensis) of Rufous-vented Grass Babbler appears intermediate in phenotype with [the bird], and further research is required to understand whether the two species need to be reunited taxonomically. Subspecies Monotypic, but further research on [the bird] burnesii nepalicola is required.

Option B is correct as it was later lumped with Rufous-vented Grass Babbler. Option C is incorrect because phylogenetic studies removed it from Sylviidae and placed it in [the bird] (a babbler family). Option D is correct as it is described as monotypic. Option E is correct due to mention of the new subspecies nepalicola possibly leading to reunification.

options.D: It is currently considered a monotypic species with no recognized subspecies.

question: Based on the provided monograph, which of the following statements are correct regarding the taxonomy and phylogeny of Zosterops melanurus?

exact_quote: A recent split from the formerly large wastebasket taxon Oriental White-eye (Z. palpebrosus), this small white-eye is now considered endemic to Java and Bali, with an unconfirmed population in Sumatra. Two subspecies are currently recognized, and both are very different from each other: the yellow-bellied melanurus occurs in the eastern part of West Java all the way to East Java, and the gray-bellied buxtoni occurs on the western tip of West Java. Both populations are known to overlap in some areas around Mount Gede-Pangrango, with some evidence of interbreeding where they co-occur. Despite their differences, the two populations share several characteristics, including an olive-green head, back, and wing, a yellowish rump, and blackish-brown flight-feathers and tail. The species is known to occur in many types of habitat, from evergreen and deciduous forest all the way to rural or even urban areas (including in the Indonesian capital city of Jakarta); however, they are increasingly difficult to find around human habitation, most likely due to the rampant trapping for the caged-bird trade. The demand for this bird (and other white-eye species) suddenly increased in early 2010, fueled by the emergence of its own category in bird-singing contests―a common pastime for people across Java and Bali. The [the bird] is considered to be one of the most heavily-traded bird species in Java and Bali, with 6,884 individuals reported in snapshot surveys of several bird markets across Java and Bali between 2014-2018. While still described as common in some areas (especially in protected areas), the [the bird] is now listed as Vulnurable (VU) by the IUCN.
provenance.reasoning_chain: Option A is correct: The text explicitly states '[the bird]' was recently split from Oriental White-eye (Z. palpebrosus). Option C is correct: The text mentions that subspecies melanurus and buxtoni consistently grouped together in a well-supported clade. Option E is correct: The text states close relationships of '[the bird]' are still not fully resolved and that relationships with other species are not well supported. Option B is incorrect: The text mentions Lemon-bellied White-eye (Z. chloris) as a similar species but does not state it is a sister species; in fact, it suggests possible co-existence in Bali Barat but no phylogenetic relationship is mentioned. Option D is incorrect: While the text mentions overlap with Warbling White-eye (Z. japonicus) in some areas, it does not state they are closely related or frequently hybridize; hybridization is mentioned only between the two subspecies of '[the bird]'.

options.A: It was recently split from the Oriental White-eye (Z. palpebrosus) based on molecular evidence.
options.B: It is considered a sister species to the Lemon-bellied White-eye (Z. chloris).
options.C: The two recognized subspecies (melanurus and buxtoni) form a well-supported clade distinct from other white-eye species.
options.D: It is closely related to the Warbling White-eye (Z. japonicus), with which it frequently hybridizes.
options.E: Its relationships with other white-eye species (e.g., Indian White-eye, Ashy-bellied White-eye) are not fully resolved and lack strong support.

question: Based on the provided text, which of the following descriptions accurately characterize the locomotion and social behaviors of Sitta pygmaea? Select ALL correct answers.

exact_quote:
Moves quickly compared with creeper or woodpecker. Habitually hops both up and down all parts of tree, head first, without using tail feathers for support. Moves both right-side up and upside-down. Upper foot clings, with “sole” of foot pulled away from surface. Lower foot supports body, with “sole” depressed against trunk (Figure 3). It positions leg socket dorsally so that front end of body pivots out from trunk of tree, a position that individual often takes when it pauses. Going down, bird uses only 1 toe for grasping; going up, it uses 3 (Law 1929c Law, J. E. (1929c). Down-tree progress of [the bird]. Condor 31:45-51. Close ). Laterally compressed claws, a relatively large hallux directed posteriorly, with the other 3 digits directed forward, facilitate head-down movements in this and other nuthatch species (see also Zippelius 1973 Zippelius, H. M. (1973). Das Kopfabwärtsklettern des Kleibers ([the bird] europaea). Bonner zoologische Beiträge 24:48. Close ).

Gregarious and social throughout year. [the bird]es almost invariably occur in flocks. Size and thermodynamics of roost cavities may limit group size (Sydeman et al. 1988 Sydeman, W. J., M. Güntert and R. P. Balda. (1988). Annual reproductive yield in the cooperative [the bird] ([the bird]). Auk 105:70-77. Close ). Denson (Denson 1981 Denson, R. M. (1981). The influences of selected environmental factors on the flocking behavior of [the bird]es. Master's Thesis, Northern Arizona Univ., Flagstaff. Close ) identified 5 types of flocks: Family Flock. Consisting of adults, helpers, and fledglings; average size 6.9 ± 1.3 SD individuals (n = 15). Expanded Family Flock. Coalescence of several Family Flocks. Depending on season, mean size ranges from 6.9 to 9.8 birds ± 1.3–3.6 SD. Flock forms in late fall or early winter and maintains relatively strong association until pairing occurs in early spring. Multiple Family Flock. Temporary associations of ≥2 Expanded Family Flocks that come together at mutual flock boundaries. These stay together for minutes or all day. Depending on season, mean flock size ranges from 7.0 to 25.6 ± 0.8–7.9 SD. Roost Flock. Enlarges over the year from Family to Expanded Family flocks; occasionally several Expanded Family Flocks roost together, even though during the day, they forage separately with minimal contact. See Self-maintenance, above. Interspecific Flock. At least 17 species identified as flock associates. Depending on season, mean flock size ranges from 12.9 to 15.4 ± 6.9–10.5 SD. See Flock behavior, below. Flocks largest Nov–Jan, with peak in Dec (McEllin 1978 McEllin, S. M. (1978). Adaptive accommodations of nuthatches in ponderosa pine forests. question: Based on the description provided, which of the following statements accurately describe the physical characteristics of Aplonis brunneicapillus?

question: Based on the provided monograph, which of the following descriptions are correct regarding the breeding ecology of Leucopsar rothschildi?

exact_quote: Breeding Breeds during rainy season, Jan–Apr. Nest a lining of dry twigs, placed by both sexes in natural tree hole, particularly old hole of woodpecker (Picidae), 4–10 m above ground; nestboxes used in captivity. Clutch 2–3 eggs, in captivity usually 3; eggs pale blue, rarely with faint brown spots; incubation mainly by female, period 12–15 days; chicks brooded by female, fed by both parents, nestling period generally 22–24 days, in captivity up to 28 days; young fed by parents for up to 7 weeks after leaving nest, although start to feed themselves at 4–5 weeks. Hatching success in captivity 68%; productivity low, as normally only one chick survives to fledging stage. Captive females more than 11 years old no longer lay eggs.
provenance.reasoning_chain: Option A is correct because the quote states 'Nest a lining of dry twigs, placed by both sexes in natural tree hole'. Option B is incorrect as the clutch size is 2-3 eggs, not 4-5, and incubation period is 12-15 days, not 18-20. Option C is correct as it directly matches 'Breeds during rainy season, Jan–Apr'. Option D is correct as it matches 'nestling period generally 22–24 days, in captivity up to 28 days; chicks brooded by female, fed by both parents'. Option E is incorrect because the quote explicitly states 'Captive females more than 11 years old no longer lay eggs'.

options.A: Both sexes participate in nest construction, typically using natural tree holes.
options.B: The clutch size is usually 4-5 eggs, which are incubated for 18-20 days.
options.C: The breeding season occurs during the rainy months, primarily from January to April.
options.D: Nestling period generally lasts 22-24 days, with chicks fed by both parents.
options.E: Captive females older than 11 years continue to lay eggs regularly.

Formerly widespread on Negros, but since 1980 only recorded at two sites, Ban-ban and Mambucal; continuing habitat clearance and destruction may now have eliminated these populations.
provenance.reasoning_chain: Option A is correct as the text explicitly states the distribution includes Panay, Guimaras, and Negros in WC Philippines. Option B is incorrect as the distribution is restricted to these three islands, not the entire archipelago. Option C is correct as the text states it was last recorded on Guimaras in 1887 and is presumed extinct there. Option D is incorrect as the text states it is a resident species, not migratory. Option E is correct as the text specifies that since 1980, it has only been recorded at two sites on Negros: Ban-ban and Mambucal.

options.A: It is found on the islands of Panay, Guimaras, and Negros in the western central Philippines.
options.B: It is a widespread species found throughout the entire Philippine archipelago.
options.C: It is presumed extinct on the island of Guimaras, where it was last recorded in 1887.
options.D: It is a migratory species that moves seasonally between the Philippines and mainland Asia.
options.E: On Negros, it has been recorded at only two sites (Ban-ban and Mambucal) since 1980.

question: Based on the provided monograph, which of the following statements accurately describe the general behavior of Oenanthe fusca?

Option D is correct as it notes 'Recorded feeding during the night on insects attracted to bright sodium lamps.' question: Based on the provided monograph, which of the following statements accurately describe the breeding ecology of Saxicola rubetra? Select ALL correct descriptions.

exact_quote: Breeding Mid-Apr to early Aug in NW Europe. Territory less than 1 ha, average 0·43 ha in Netherlands, at least 0·75 ha in W Germany; site-fidelity among adults high (of 54 breeding males, 47% returned to same area after one year, 15% for two years and 4% for three years, and almost half of all these reoccupied same territory). Nest a cup of grass stems, leaves and moss, lined with fine stems and hair, placed in low bush or tussock. Eggs 4–7, pale blue with fine reddish-brown speckling; incubation period 12–13 days; nestling period 12–13 days, although young not capable of flight until 17–19 days; post-fledging dependence 15–18 days.
provenance.reasoning_chain: Option A is correct as the quote explicitly describes the nest as 'a cup of grass stems, leaves and moss, lined with fine stems and hair, placed in low bush or tussock.' Option C is correct as the quote states 'Breeding Mid-Apr to early Aug in NW Europe.' Option D is correct as the quote specifies 'Eggs 4–7, pale blue with fine reddish-brown speckling.' Option B is incorrect because while the incubation and nestling periods are 12-13 days, the quote clarifies that young are 'not capable of flight until 17–19 days,' not immediately after fledging. Option E is incorrect because the quote indicates 'site-fidelity among adults is high,' not low, with detailed return rates provided.

options.A: The nest is constructed as a cup made of grass stems, leaves, moss, and lined with fine stems and hair, placed in a low bush or tussock.
options.B: The incubation period is 12-13 days, and the nestling period is 12-13 days, with young capable of flight immediately after fledging.
options.C: The breeding season in northwestern Europe extends from mid-April to early August.
options.D: Eggs are typically 4-7 in number, pale blue with fine reddish-brown speckling.
options.E: Territory size averages 0.43 hectares in the Netherlands, and site-fidelity among adults is low, with most birds changing territories annually.

question: Based on the provided monograph, which of the following statements about the taxonomy and phylogeny of Stiphrornis erythrothorax are correct?

exact_quote: Subspecies gabonensis differs from nominate in its dark gray versus olive-brown crown to tail; and looser song phrases, with slightly longer notes. Subspecies dahomeyensis and inexpectatus, described very recently as phylogenetic species, have not been scored using the Tobias et al. criteria, but morphological differences are obviously rather minor, and are here both considered junior synonyms of erythrothorax. In a molecular phylogeny using mitochondrial DNA sequence data, [the bird] appears to be sister to Yellow-breasted Forest Robin ([the bird] mabirae), which are together sister to Olive-backed Forest Robin ([the bird] pyrrholaemus). The type locality of xanthogaster is the Dja River in southwestern Cameroon, and so xanthogaster here is restricted to the western Congo Basin, whereas birds previously assigned to xanthogaster from the eastern Congo Basin, including Uganda and the Democratic Republic of Congo, are here treated as Yellow-breasted Forest Robin ([the bird] mabirae).
provenance.reasoning_chain: Option A is correct as the text states gabonensis differs from nominate in crown/tail color and song phrases. Option C is correct as dahomeyensis and inexpectatus are considered junior synonyms of erythrothorax due to minor morphological differences. Option D is correct as the phylogeny shows [the bird] is sister to Yellow-breasted Forest Robin, and together they are sister to Olive-backed Forest Robin. Option B is incorrect because xanthogaster is restricted to the western Congo Basin, not the eastern Congo Basin (which is treated as Yellow-breasted Forest Robin). Option E is incorrect because the text indicates subspecies were not found sufficiently different to warrant species status using quantitative criteria, and some subspecies like dahomeyensis/inexpectatus have not been scored with these criteria.

options.A: The subspecies gabonensis differs from the nominate subspecies in having a dark gray versus olive-brown crown to tail and looser song phrases.
options.B: The subspecies xanthogaster is restricted to the eastern Congo Basin, including Uganda and the Democratic Republic of Congo.
options.C: The subspecies dahomeyensis and inexpectatus are considered junior synonyms of erythrothorax due to minor morphological differences.
options.D: In molecular phylogeny, [the bird] appears to be sister to Yellow-breasted Forest Robin, and together they are sister to Olive-backed Forest Robin.
options.E: All recognized subspecies of [the bird] have been confirmed to warrant full species status based on quantitative criteria for species delimitation.

question: Based on the provided text, which of the following statements accurately describe conservation threats or status information for Sheppardia gabela?

exact_quote: Conservation status on Birdlife EN Endangered ENDANGERED. Restricted-range species: present in Western Angola EBA. Known only from 60-km stretch of escarpment between Gabela and Seles. Global population in range 1000–2500 mature individuals; considered to be declining as its habitat diminishes in extent and quality. Loss of habitat to subsistence agriculture a threat, 20–70% of canopy trees and all undergrowth in valley bottoms being cleared in some areas for bananas and sweet potatoes, and elsewhere up to 90% of canopy being removed for cassava and maize cultivation. Practice of clearing forest understorey for coffee probably robs this species of an essential habitat component, although it occurs in overgrown coffee neglected for c. 30 years. A protected area of 50 km² within its range was proposed in early 1970s, but never implemented.
provenance.reasoning_chain: Option A is correct as the text states the bird is Endangered with a global population of 1000-2500 mature individuals and declining. Option B is correct as the text lists clearing for bananas, sweet potatoes, cassava, and maize as threats from subsistence agriculture. Option C is incorrect because the text says the protected area was 'proposed... but never implemented,' not successfully established. Option D is correct as the text indicates clearing understorey for coffee 'probably robs this species of an essential habitat component.' Option E is correct as the text specifies the bird is 'known only from 60-km stretch of escarpment between Gabela and Seles.'

options.A: It is classified as Endangered due to a declining global population of 1000-2500 mature individuals.
options.B: Its habitat is threatened by clearing for subsistence agriculture including bananas, sweet potatoes, cassava, and maize.
options.C: A protected area of 50 km² within its range was successfully established in the early 1970s.
options.D: Clearing forest understorey for coffee cultivation removes an essential habitat component for this species.
options.E: It is found only in a 60-km stretch of escarpment between Gabela and Seles in Western Angola.

question: Based on the distribution information provided, which of the following statements are correct regarding where Chamaetylas choloensis is found?

exact_quote: The [the bird] is found in southeastern Malawi and adjacent northwestern Mozambique where it occurs in submontane and montane forest in a small number of isolated mountains at 950–1,900 m and locally down to 700–900 m. Recorded at the Following Sites in Malawi: Mount Mulanje recorded in 1936 and 1983–84. Most recent records are from Ruo and Chisongeli Forests on the southern slopes where the species was graphed in 2019 and 2023. Recorded at the Following Sites in Mozambique: Mount Namuli at 1,200–1,700 m, where it is common in the Ukalini Forest but much less so in the larger and cooler block of Manho Forest. Mount Mabu where the [the bird] is numerous and covers a wide altitudinal range of 950–1,650 m. It was previously more widespread in southeastern Malawi, and probably also in Mozambique, but forest clearance has destroyed many submontane forests where it occurred, especially in the Shire Highlands close to the town Blantyre and in the Thyolo Mountains. Forest clearance has since reduced its range significantly, and it has probably disappeared from most if not all of the forests of the Shire Highlands near Blantyre town.
provenance.reasoning_chain: Option A is correct as the text states the bird is found in southeastern Malawi and adjacent northwestern Mozambique in submontane and montane forests. Option B is correct as the text specifies elevations of 950–1,900 m and locally down to 700–900 m. Option C is correct as the text lists Mount Mulanje in Malawi and Mount Namuli in Mozambique as recorded sites. Option D is incorrect because the text says it has probably disappeared from most if not all forests in the Shire Highlands due to forest clearance. Option E is correct as the text states Mount Mabu in Mozambique has numerous birds covering a wide altitudinal range of 950–1,650 m.

options.A: It occurs in submontane and montane forests in southeastern Malawi and adjacent northwestern Mozambique.
options.B: It is found at elevations ranging from 950–1,900 m, but has been recorded locally down to 700–900 m.
options.C: It has been recorded on Mount Mulanje in Malawi and Mount Namuli in Mozambique.
options.D: It is present in all forested areas of the Shire Highlands near Blantyre town in Malawi.
options.E: It occurs on Mount Mabu in Mozambique, where it is numerous and covers a wide altitudinal range.

question: Based on the provided text, which of the following statements accurately describe the historical and current distribution of Saxicola macrorhynchus? Select all that apply.

exact_quote: The [the bird] occurs in sandy semi-desert, semiarid grasslands, and desert areas with scattered shrubs, and is now virtually endemic to Northwest India, though it formerly also occurred in Pakistan and Afghanistan. Recent summer records are primarily from Rajasthan (India), particularly the Thar Desert, where it remains widespread at low densities. In the nonbreeding period, it also has been recorded from Haryana and Gujarat (particularly in the modern day Kachchh District) and whether it breeds in these locations remains unknown. There are also recent records from Maharashtra, suggesting that much remains to be learned about its nonbreeding distribution. Has undergone a considerable decline and range contraction during the 1900s. There are no recent records from Afghanistan and Pakistan, and current records are all from Northwest India.
provenance.reasoning_chain: Option A is correct as the text states it is 'now virtually endemic to Northwest India' and 'recent summer records are primarily from Rajasthan'. Option B is correct as it 'formerly also occurred in Pakistan and Afghanistan' and 'there are no recent records from Afghanistan and Pakistan'. Option D is correct as it has been recorded from 'Haryana and Gujarat' and 'recent records from Maharashtra'. Option C is incorrect because it is not found breeding across all of India, and there is no mention of Tamil Nadu; it is primarily in Northwest India and rare elsewhere. Option E is incorrect because the text indicates a decline and range contraction, not expansion, due to habitat conversion and canal irrigation.

options.A: It is now virtually endemic to Northwest India, with recent summer records primarily from Rajasthan.
options.B: It historically occurred in Pakistan and Afghanistan, but there are no recent records from these countries.
options.C: It is currently found breeding in large numbers across all of India, including southern states like Tamil Nadu.
options.D: Recent nonbreeding records include sightings in Haryana, Gujarat, and Maharashtra.
options.E: Its range has expanded significantly due to habitat conversion and canal irrigation in the 20th century.

question: Based on the provided monograph, which of the following statements accurately describe the conservation status and threats faced by Myophonus blighi?

exact_quote: Conservation status on Birdlife EN Endangered ENDANGERED. Restricted-range species: present in Sri Lanka EBA. Always considered scarce, and now thought to possess declining, increasingly fragmented population consisting of 1000–2500 mature individuals. In recent review, 26 localities mapped, of which only ten known to involve post-1980 records; available forest habitat, of which only areas near streams suitable, covers only 700 km². Threats include clearance of habitat, even some protected forests, through conversion to timber plantations and agriculture, compounded by die-back in some areas (perhaps owing to air pollution), and degradation of habitat through firewood collection, gem-mining and pesticide chemical run-off from vegetable farms, which pollutes streams within its range. Even tape playback by visiting birdwatchers may overly disturb breeding birds at Horton Plains National Park. Other protected areas with populations of this species include Peak Wilderness Sanctuary and Hakgala Strict Nature Reserve. Comprehensive survey and assessment of threats needed. Legally protected.
provenance.reasoning_chain: Option A is correct as the text explicitly states the bird is Endangered with a declining population of 1000–2500 mature individuals. Option C is correct because the text lists habitat clearance for timber plantations and agriculture, and die-back possibly due to air pollution as threats. Option E is correct as the text mentions habitat degradation from firewood collection, gem-mining, and pesticide run-off from vegetable farms. Option B is incorrect because the text specifies conversion to timber plantations and agriculture, not urban development or industrial zones. Option D is incorrect as the text states 26 localities mapped with only ten having post-1980 records, not over 50 localities with most having such records.

options.A: It is classified as Endangered with a declining population of 1000–2500 mature individuals.
options.B: Its habitat is primarily threatened by conversion to urban development and industrial zones.
options.C: Threats include habitat clearance for timber plantations and agriculture, as well as die-back possibly due to air pollution.
options.D: It is found in over 50 localities across its range, with most having post-1980 records.
options.E: Additional threats involve habitat degradation from firewood collection, gem-mining, and pesticide run-off from vegetable farms.

question: Based on the provided text, which of the following statements accurately describe the plumage characteristics of Larvivora komadori? Select ALL correct options.

exact_quote: Definitive Basic (Adult) Plumage Female. Upperparts are rufous, similar to those of the adult male, but duller and slightly paler, especially the fringes to the remiges, which are almost yellowish orange. Lacks all black in the plumage; instead, the forehead is brown (often streaked paler), and the lores and lower face are whitish with fine streaks/smudges of gray. The sides of the lower throat and edge of the upper breast may form something of a gray gorget, but the rest of the underparts are white, as in adult male. Male. Upper forehead, nape, ear coverts, upperparts and uppertail coverts, scapulars, wings, and tail are bright rufous. Edges of the remiges are rufous, but slightly paler on the fringes to the primaries and inner webs of greater coverts, and dark gray tertials. The inner webs of the primary coverts are rufous, becoming dark gray on the center of the inner webs. Lower forehead, ear-coverts, lores, chin, and throat to mid-breast are jet black. The rest of the underparts are white (or whitish), except for large black smudges on the flanks. Juvenile Plumage The juvenile male has blackish feather bases with whitish to grayish tips, but is otherwise like first-winter birds.
provenance.reasoning_chain: Option A is correct: The quote states adult males have 'bright rufous' (synonymous with orange in context) upperparts and 'jet black' on lower forehead, ear-coverts, lores, chin, throat to mid-breast, with 'large black smudges on the flanks'. Option B is incorrect: Females have 'rufous' upperparts that are 'duller and slightly paler' than males, not identical. Option C is correct: Females have 'rufous' upperparts 'duller and slightly paler' and 'lacks all black in the plumage', with underparts white. Option D is correct: Juvenile males have 'blackish feather bases with whitish to grayish tips' and are 'otherwise like first-winter birds'. Option E is incorrect: Males have 'large black smudges on the flanks', so underparts are not entirely white.

options.A: Adult males have bright orange upperparts and a jet-black face, throat, breast, and flanks.
options.B: Adult females have bright orange upperparts identical to males but lack any black plumage.
options.C: Adult females have rufous upperparts that are duller and slightly paler than males, with whitish underparts and no black plumage.
options.D: Juvenile males resemble first-winter birds but have blackish feather bases with whitish to grayish tips.
options.E: Adult males have entirely white underparts without any black markings on the flanks.

Subspecies SUBSPECIES [the bird] aeneum Scientific name definitions D. a. aeneum +1 D. a. aeneum +1 Distribution N and C Solomons (Buka, Bougainville, Fauro, Shortland, Choiseul, Santa Isabel, Buena Vista, Florida Is). SUBSPECIES [the bird] becki Scientific name definitions Distribution Guadalcanal, in SW Solomons. SUBSPECIES [the bird] malaitae Scientific name definitions D. a. malaitae +1 D. a. malaitae +1 Distribution Malaita I, in E Solomons. In study using mtDNA markers (1 Smith, C.E. and Filardi, C.E. (2007). Patterns of molecular and morphological variation in some Solomon Island land birds. Auk 124(2): 479–493. Close ), up to at least 7% difference found between subspecies. Race malaitae the most divergent genetically, and notably distinctive for its thinner, longer bill (2 Salomonsen, F. (1960). Notes on flowerpeckers (Aves, [the bird]). 3. The species group [the bird] concolor and the superspecies [the bird] erythrothorax. Amer. Mus. Novit. 2016: 1–36. Close ), suggesting different ecology, although plumage differences seemingly minor; study of voice required (3 Boesman, P. (2016). Notes on the vocalizations of [the bird] ([the bird]). HBW Alive Ornithological Note 336. In: Handbook of the Birds of the World Alive. Lynx Edicions, Barcelona. Close ).
provenance.reasoning_chain: Option A is correct because the text explicitly states 'Three subspecies recognized' and lists aeneum, becki, and malaitae. Option B is correct as the text notes 'up to at least 7% difference found between subspecies' and 'Race malaitae the most divergent genetically'. Option C is correct based on earlier text in the 'Identification' section: 'becki male has greenish gloss above, rather than the blue of nominate'. Option D is incorrect because aeneum is distributed in 'N and C Solomons', not only Guadalcanal (which is the distribution of becki). Option E is incorrect as malaitae has a 'thinner, longer bill' and a 'study of voice required' implies vocalizations may differ.

options.A: Three subspecies are recognized: aeneum, becki, and malaitae.
options.B: The subspecies malaitae is the most genetically divergent, with up to at least 7% difference in mtDNA markers compared to other subspecies.
options.C: The subspecies becki has a greenish gloss on the dorsal surface, while the nominate race has a blue gloss.
options.D: The subspecies aeneum is found only on the island of Guadalcanal in the Solomon Islands.
options.E: All subspecies of [the bird] have identical bill morphology and vocalizations.

question: Based on the provided monograph, which of the following descriptions accurately characterize the morphology or identification features of Deleornis fraseri? Select all that apply.

exact_quote: A large dull green sunbird , with long straight bill curved only at tip. Male nominate race is uniformly bright olive-green above, with upperwing and tail brown, outer webs edged yellow-olive; yellow-olive below, pectoral tufts orange-red with yellow at base, axillaries pale yellow, underwing-coverts greyish-white; iris hazel, pale yellow or white eyering; bill dull brown, base of lower mandible olive-yellow; legs olive, claws yellowish-horn. Distinguished from Cinnyris batesi and Anthreptes seimundi and from female of Anthreptes rectirostris mainly by long straight bill (curved only at very tip) and presence of pectoral tufts. Female is as male, but smaller and without pectoral tufts. Juvenile differs from adult in being all pale olive above, paler below, with yellow wash on belly, darker bill. Race cameroonensis has duller olive-green underparts with less yellow tinge than nominate; idius is smallest and darkest, with darker brown (less green) tail, also iris reddish-brown, upper mandible horn, lower mandible yellowish-horn, and legs greenish-slate with pinkish claws.
provenance.reasoning_chain: Option A is correct as the text explicitly states the bill is 'long straight bill curved only at tip' and that this feature helps distinguish it from other species. Option B is correct because the male has 'pectoral tufts orange-red with yellow at base' and the female 'is as male, but smaller and without pectoral tufts'. Option D is correct as the juvenile is described as 'all pale olive above, paler below, with yellow wash on belly, darker bill'. Option C is incorrect because the race cameroonensis has 'duller olive-green underparts with less yellow tinge than nominate', indicating variation among subspecies. Option E is incorrect because the iris color varies: it is 'hazel' for the nominate race, but for idius it is 'reddish-brown', showing inconsistency across subspecies.

options.A: It has a long straight bill that is curved only at the tip, which helps distinguish it from similar species.
options.B: The male possesses orange-red pectoral tufts with yellow at the base, while the female lacks these tufts.
options.C: All subspecies have uniformly bright olive-green underparts with a strong yellow tinge.
options.D: The juvenile is distinguished by being all pale olive above, paler below, with a yellow wash on the belly and a darker bill.
options.E: Its iris color is consistently hazel across all subspecies and age groups.

question: Based on the provided description, which of the following statements are correct regarding the identification of Chalcomitra amethystina?

exact_quote: Male nominate race has iridescent green patch on forehead (sometimes appears silvery light green or gold), pinkish-violet on chin and throat, and coppery-violet on carpals; rest of plumage blackish-brown except for purplish-violet uppertail-coverts and dull black upperwing, primary and greater wing-coverts and tail; some have rudimentary yellow pectoral tufts; iris dark brown; bill and legs black. Female is olive-tinged grey-brown above, slight white supercilium, uppertail-coverts dark brown, tail blackish-brown with greyish-white tips, remiges and greater wing-coverts dark greyish-brown, primaries and secondaries edged buff, paler on primaries, and lesser and median wing-coverts olive-grey; white moustachial stripe, pale grey-brown with heavy mottling below (except on belly), throat often so densely mottled as to appear black (pale moustache then especially obvious), underwing-coverts and axillaries brownish. Juvenile is similar to female but with throat blacker, and underparts more spotted and yellowish, looking barred (not streaked); immature male with iridescent rosy-purple patch on throat. Race deminuta male has shorter bill (24–28 mm) than nominate (25–32 mm), but uppertail-coverts also purplish-violet, female has throat paler, less dusky-looking (feathers lack blackish bases), underparts with variable amounts of yellow and plainer than in nominate, some with hardly any streaking; kirkii is similar to previous (smaller than nominate), but male uppertail-coverts blackish-brown or dull black, lacking metallic purplish-violet.
provenance.reasoning_chain: Option A is correct as the quote states the male nominate has an 'iridescent green patch on forehead' and 'purplish-violet uppertail-coverts'. Option B is incorrect because the female's throat is described as 'often so densely mottled as to appear black', not pale and unmarked. Option C is correct as the quote says the juvenile is 'similar to female but with throat blacker, and underparts more spotted'. Option D is incorrect because race deminuta males have a 'shorter bill (24–28 mm) than nominate (25–32 mm)'. Option E is correct as the quote specifies that race kirkii males have 'uppertail-coverts blackish-brown or dull black, lacking metallic purplish-violet'.

options.A: The male nominate race has iridescent green on the forehead and purplish-violet uppertail-coverts.
options.B: The female has a distinct white supercilium and a pale, unmarked throat.
options.C: The juvenile resembles the female but has a blacker throat and more spotted underparts.
options.D: Race deminuta males have a longer bill than the nominate race.
options.E: Race kirkii males lack the metallic purplish-violet uppertail-coverts found in the nominate race.

question: Based on the provided monograph, which of the following statements correctly describe the recognized subspecies of Dicaeum maugei?

exact_quote: Proposed race mariae (from Nusa Penida, off SE Bali) synonymized with neglectum; romae (from Roma I) considered indistinguishable from nominate. Four subspecies recognized. Subspecies SUBSPECIES [the bird] splendidum Scientific name definitions D. m. splendidum Distribution Selayar and Tanahjampea, S of Sulawesi. SUBSPECIES [the bird] neglectum Scientific name definitions Distribution Nusa Penida (off SE Bali) and Lombok, in W Lesser Sundas. SUBSPECIES [the bird] maugei Scientific name definitions D. m. maugei +1 D. m. maugei +1 Distribution Sawu, Roti, Semau, Timor, Atauro, Wetar, Romang and Damar, in E Lesser Sundas. SUBSPECIES [the bird] salvadorii Scientific name definitions Distribution Moa and Babar, in extreme E Lesser Sundas.
provenance.reasoning_chain: Option A is correct because the text explicitly states 'Four subspecies recognized' and lists neglectum and salvadorii among them. Option B is correct as it directly quotes the distribution for splendidum. Option D is correct as it states mariae is synonymized with neglectum. Option C is incorrect because maugei is only in the E Lesser Sundas, not the entire range. Option E is incorrect because romae is considered indistinguishable from nominate, not distinct.

options.A: Four subspecies are recognized, including neglectum and salvadorii.
options.B: The subspecies splendidum is found on Selayar and Tanahjampea, south of Sulawesi.
options.C: The subspecies maugei is distributed across the entire Lesser Sundas, from Bali to Timor.
options.D: The proposed race mariae from Nusa Penida is considered a synonym of neglectum.
options.E: The subspecies romae from Roma I is recognized as distinct from the nominate race.

question: Based on the provided description, which of the following statements are correct regarding the physical characteristics of Dicaeum erythrorhynchos?

exact_quote: Nominate race is plain greyish-brown or olive-brown above, remiges dark brown with pale edging, rectrices dark brown with pale tips; lores and side of face paler; sandy grey to greyish-white below, sometimes tinged greyish-brown on sides of breast, and often more buffy on belly and flanks, whitish underwing-coverts; iris hazel-brown; bill pale horn-brown , pinkish-flesh at gape and on lower mandible except tip, mouth pale pink; legs dark slate-coloured. Sexes similar. Juvenile is greyer above and below than adult, with shorter bill orange-yellow at gape and on lower mandible (except tip). Race ceylonense is smaller, darker, more olive above and below, than nominate, with bill plumbeous-brown, or silvery or pinkish with dark culmen, lower mandible dark brown, and iris yellowish-brown.
provenance.reasoning_chain: Option A is correct as the text states the nominate race has 'bill pale horn-brown, pinkish-flesh at gape and on lower mandible except tip'. Option C is correct as it describes race ceylonense as 'smaller, darker, more olive above and below, than nominate'. Option E is correct as it notes the nominate race has 'rectrices dark brown with pale tips' and 'remiges dark brown with pale edging'. Option B is incorrect because the juvenile has a 'shorter bill', not longer. Option D is incorrect because the iris of race ceylonense is 'yellowish-brown', not consistently hazel-brown.

options.A: The nominate race has a pale horn-brown bill with pinkish-flesh coloration at the gape and on the lower mandible except the tip.
options.B: The juvenile has a longer bill than the adult, with orange-yellow coloration at the gape and on the lower mandible except the tip.
options.C: The race ceylonense is smaller, darker, and more olive above and below compared to the nominate race.
options.D: The iris color is consistently hazel-brown across all age groups and subspecies.
options.E: The nominate race has dark brown rectrices with pale tips and dark brown remiges with pale edging.

question: Based on the provided description, which of the following are accurate statements about the plumage and physical characteristics of Prionochilus xanthopygius?

exact_quote: Male has slate-blue head, back, upperwing and tail, red patch on crown , yellow rump; yellow below, orange patch on upper breast , white pectoral tufts (concealed), flanks olive and grey, undertail-coverts yellowish-white, underwing-coverts white; iris brown; bill and legs black. Femalevideo is duller than male, has blue-grey crown with very small dull orange-red patch, greenish-olive back, yellow rump; throat whitish, side of face grey, flanks olive-grey, undertail-coverts whitish, rest of underparts yellow, some orange on upper breast. Juvenile is similar to female, but more bluish-tinged grey above, uppertail-coverts olive, yellow of rump less distinct, upperwing and tail blackish-brown, wing feathers edged blue-grey; much greyer below, with almost no yellow; bill pale.
provenance.reasoning_chain: Option A is correct as it accurately describes the male's slate-blue head, back, upperwing, tail, red crown patch, and yellow rump. Option C is correct as it matches the description of the juvenile being similar to the female but with more bluish-tinged grey above and much greyer underparts with almost no yellow. Option E is correct as it states the male's iris is brown and bill and legs are black. Option B is incorrect because the female's crown patch is described as 'very small dull orange-red,' not 'large bright orange-red.' Option D is incorrect because the white pectoral tufts in males are described as 'concealed,' not always prominently displayed, and there is no mention of them in females.

options.A: The male has a slate-blue head, back, upperwing, and tail, with a red patch on the crown and a yellow rump.
options.B: The female has a blue-grey crown with a large bright orange-red patch and a greenish-olive back.
options.C: The juvenile is similar to the female but has a more bluish-tinged grey above and much greyer underparts with almost no yellow.
options.D: Both males and females have white pectoral tufts that are always prominently displayed.
options.E: The iris is brown, and the bill and legs are black in the male.

question: Based on the provided monograph, which of the following statements accurately describe the physical characteristics of Ploceus holoxanthus? Select ALL correct descriptions.

exact_quote: The [the bird] has a dark brown eye in both sexes, while the male African Golden-Weaver has a reddish eye all year. The male [the bird] is also more yellow above, with a slight olive wash, while African Golden-Weaver has an olive back that is noticeably different to its yellow underparts. The primaries of [the bird] are largely yellow, while the wings of African Golden-Weaver are pale olive with a yellow outer border. The female [the bird] has a distinctive two-toned bill color, with the maxilla being dark dusky-gray and the mandible being pale yellowish-orange, and is grayish white on the belly, while the female African Golden-Weaver has a horn colored bill and is yellowish below (breeding) or whitish below (non breeding).

Option B is correct: The text explicitly describes the female's two-toned bill with dark maxilla and pale mandible. Option C is incorrect: The text says the male [the bird] has a dark brown eye, while the male African Golden-Weaver has reddish eyes. Option D is incorrect: This describes the female African Golden-Weaver, not [the bird]. Option E is correct: The text directly compares the primaries of [the bird] (largely yellow) with African Golden-Weaver (pale olive with yellow outer border).

options.A: The male has a bright yellow body with an orange face and a dark brown eye.
options.B: The female has a two-toned bill, with the maxilla being dark dusky-gray and the mandible being pale yellowish-orange.
options.C: The male has reddish eyes during the breeding season, similar to the African Golden-Weaver.
options.D: The female has a horn-colored bill and is yellowish below during breeding.
options.E: The primaries of [the bird] are largely yellow, while the wings of African Golden-Weaver are pale olive with a yellow outer border.

question: Based on the provided monograph, which of the following behaviors are accurately described for Euplectes nigroventris?

Territory size variable, from 120–240 m2 in open grassland and up to 800 m2 in bulrushes (Typha) to smaller than 10 m2 in Phragmites reeds; defends territory against E. hordeaceus, whereas E. ardens and E. albonotatus apparently tolerated.

Option C is incorrect because the text indicates [the bird] is mainly resident with some local movements, not long-distance migration. Option E is incorrect as the nest is described as made from grass strips and lined with seedheads, not mud and twigs, and is placed in grass, reeds, or bushes, not high in trees.

question: Based on the provided description, which of the following are accurate statements about the plumage and physical characteristics of Ploceus grandis?

exact_quote: Male has most of head down to chin and throat black, blending into chestnut-brown on rear crown ; mantle to upper back dull greenish yellow with thin dark central streaks, lower back and rump dull yellow; tail and upperwing dark olive-green, tertials and wing-coverts with yellow edges, wing-coverts also with yellow tips (forming wingbars); chestnut-brown band across breast linked to similar-coloured area on nape; flanks yellow, washed with chestnut-brown, belly, thighs and undertail-coverts yellow; iris yellow; bill black; legs brown. question: Based on the provided monograph, which of the following statements correctly describe aspects of the breeding ecology of Foudia rubra?

exact_quote: Breeding Season Oct–Feb. Monogamous. Occupies permanent territory 4–5 ha in size in sparsely populated areas, or down to as small as 0–9 ha where more common. Nest domed, with side entrance and often porch, built primarily from grass with moss, lichens or small twigs, lined with down feathers, placed 2–9 m above ground in tree; division of work unclear, as both sexes seen to carry material, but in some cases female did most building. Clutch 2–3 eggs , pale blue, average size of ten eggs 19–2 x 13–9 mm; incubation apparently by female only, period reported as 14 days; chicks fed by both sexes, nestling period recorded as 18 days.
provenance.reasoning_chain: The exact quote supports options A, C, D, and E: A is correct as the breeding season is Oct–Feb; C is correct as the clutch is 2-3 pale blue eggs with average size 19.2 x 13.9 mm (note: '19–2 x 13–9 mm' in the text is interpreted as 19.2 x 13.9 mm based on standard notation); D is correct as incubation is by female only for 14 days; E is correct as chicks are fed by both sexes for 18 days. Option B is incorrect because the text states the nest is built primarily from grass with moss, lichens, or small twigs (not exclusively grass and moss), and division of work is unclear with both sexes seen carrying material, contradicting 'exclusively by the female'.

options.A: The breeding season typically occurs from October to February.
options.B: Nests are constructed exclusively by the female using only grass and moss.
options.C: The clutch size is usually 2-3 pale blue eggs, with an average size of approximately 19.2 x 13.9 mm.
options.D: Incubation is performed solely by the female and lasts about 14 days.
options.E: Nestling chicks are fed by both parents for a period recorded as 18 days.

question: Based on the provided description, which of the following statements are correct regarding the identification of Arachnothera chrysogenys?

exact_quote: Male nominate race has head and upperparts olive-green, suffused golden on mantle, becoming brighter on rump, with large yellow cheek patch and narrow yellow filoplume eyering, much narrower on lower half; edges of remiges bright yellow or golden-bronze; throat to breast yellowish-green with indistinct greenish streaks, becoming brighter yellow on belly, lower flanks and undertail-coverts; pectoral tufts grey; iris brown; bill blackish with fleshy-pink base to lower mandible and often a long central orange to yellow line along cutting edges, becoming pale grey on gape; legs dull fleshy-brown to pale brown. Female is similar to male but lacks pectoral tufts. Juvenile resembles adult, but lacks streaking and dark feather bases. Race harrissoni differs from nominate in almost completely lacking golden suffusion on mantle, which is nearly concolorous with crown, and has exposed parts of closed wing lighter and duller.
provenance.reasoning_chain: Option A is correct as the text states the male nominate has a 'large yellow cheek patch and narrow yellow filoplume eyering'. Option C is correct as it directly quotes that the 'Juvenile resembles adult, but lacks streaking and dark feather bases'. Option D is correct as it describes race harrissoni as 'almost completely lacking golden suffusion on mantle, which is nearly concolorous with crown'. Option B is incorrect because the text does not mention females having brighter yellow edges on remiges; it only states females lack pectoral tufts. Option E is incorrect because the iris is described as 'brown', not black.

options.A: The male nominate race has a large yellow cheek patch and a narrow yellow filoplume eyering.
options.B: The female differs from the male by having brighter yellow edges on the remiges.
options.C: The juvenile resembles the adult but lacks streaking and dark feather bases.
options.D: Race harrissoni has a mantle that is nearly concolorous with the crown and lacks golden suffusion.
options.E: The iris color is described as black in both sexes.

question: Based on the description provided, which of the following statements accurately describe the physical characteristics of the Aethopyga linaraborae?

exact_quote: Male has forehead metallic emerald-green with hint of blue, ear patch metallic cobalt-blue, head otherwise blackish-grey, crown feathers edged metallic blue, back olive-green with clearly defined sulphur-yellow rump, uppertail-coverts deep metallic emerald-green; tail feathers blackish-grey, edged violet, all except central feathers with whitish-silver tips; lesser and median upperwing-coverts bright metallic emerald-green, greater coverts metallic ultramarine, remiges dark brown, edges of scapulars and secondaries cobalt-blue; chin to upper breast sulphur-yellow, small orange flecks on upper breast and orange patch in centre of breast, pectoral tufts scarlet, lower breast and belly yellow, undertail-coverts sulphur-yellow, and wing-lining white (individual variation in brightness of yellow underparts and size of orange breast patch); iris dark brick-red to blood-red, skin around eye blackish-brown; bill black; legs dark brown to black, soles pale ochre-yellow. Female has more muted colours than male, and lacks metallic sheen on forehead, ear-coverts, uppertail-coverts and wing-coverts; head dark grey with trace of pale metallic emerald-green feather edges, and olive-green of back grades into olive-tinged sulphur-yellow at tail base; edges of tail feathers metallic cobalt-blue, wing-coverts olive-green, remiges edged orangey olive-yellow; throat yellowish olive-green and breast to belly yellowish-olive, all with indistinct olive-yellow streaking, diffuse orange patch on centre of lower breast and belly; bare parts as male.
provenance.reasoning_chain: Option A is correct as the text states the male has a 'forehead metallic emerald-green' and a 'clearly defined sulphur-yellow rump'. Option B is incorrect because the text specifies the female 'lacks metallic sheen on... wing-coverts'. Option C is correct as both sexes share 'iris dark brick-red to blood-red' and 'bill black' per the description of male bare parts and that female bare parts are 'as male'. Option D is correct as the male has 'small orange flecks on upper breast and orange patch in centre of breast, pectoral tufts scarlet'. Option E is incorrect because the female's throat and breast are described as having 'indistinct olive-yellow streaking', not being distinct and non-streaked.

options.A: The male has a metallic emerald-green forehead and a sulphur-yellow rump.
options.B: The female exhibits bright metallic sheen on the wing-coverts similar to the male.
options.C: Both sexes have dark brick-red to blood-red irises and black bills.
options.D: The male displays an orange patch on the center of the breast and scarlet pectoral tufts.
options.E: The female has a distinct, non-streaked yellowish-olive throat and breast.

question: Based on the provided monograph, which of the following statements accurately describe the breeding ecology of Ploceus golandi?

exact_quote: No definite information until recently, being speculated that nests might be solitary, high in trees. In 2013 the first breeding colony was found in the Dakatcha Woodlands, NW of Malindi, where c. 400–500 nests were concentrated in a small area of a tiny wetland (80 m × 30 m); nests were coarsely woven with a low side entrance, placed in the tops of tall sedges (Cyperus exaltatus) standing in water; timescale for nest-building, egg-laying, hatching and fledging was only c. 24–30 days in total (adults were displaying and nest-building on 23 Mar, and feeding young in the nest on 7 Apr, the colony being abandoned by 19 Apr).
provenance.reasoning_chain: Options B, C, and D are directly supported by the exact quote: B (400-500 nests in a small wetland area), C (nests woven with low side entrance in tall sedges in water), and D (24-30 day total breeding cycle). Option A is incorrect because the text states solitary nesting was only speculation before the colony discovery. Option E is incorrect because the text suggests breeding may occur during both rainy periods (Mar-Jun and Nov-Dec), not exclusively one.

options.A: Nests are solitary and placed high in trees.
options.B: The first breeding colony discovered contained 400-500 nests in a small wetland area.
options.C: Nests are woven with a low side entrance and placed in tall sedges standing in water.
options.D: The complete breeding cycle from nest-building to fledging takes approximately 24-30 days.
options.E: Breeding occurs exclusively during the March to June rainy period.

question: Based on the description of Aethopyga vigorsii, which of the following statements about its plumage and physical characteristics are correct?

exact_quote: Identification Male 15 cm, 7·9 g; female 10 cm, 7·7 g. Has heavy, strongly curved bill. Male has forehead to centre of crown metallic blue-green, metallic violet or blue cheek spot; nape to mantle and shoulders dark, dull crimson-red, back blackish, patch on lower back pale yellow; uppertail-coverts and elongated narrow central tail feathers blackish-brown, edged metallic blue, outer rectrices tipped dark grey, edges of other tail feathers metallic green; upperwing blackish-brown; throat to breast scarlet with obvious yellow streaks, metallic violet or blue malar streak, breast bordered below by thin blackish band which extends downwards to form narrow black patch; rest of underparts grey, underwing-coverts and axillaries white; iris red-brown to crimson; bill blackish, dark brown below; legs dark brown to blackish. Female has crown, nape and mantle greyish-olive, back olive, brightening to olive-yellow on rump and uppertail-coverts; tail black, outer webs tipped olive, inner webs tipped white, central feathers olive, wing dark brown, edged olive; chin whitish-grey, throat to breast olive-grey, rest of underparts grey, some individuals with chin to breast dull orange-scarlet; bare parts as male.
provenance.reasoning_chain: Option A is correct as the text states the male has 'forehead to centre of crown metallic blue-green, metallic violet or blue cheek spot.' Option B is correct as the female has 'crown, nape and mantle greyish-olive, back olive, brightening to olive-yellow on rump and uppertail-coverts.' Option C is correct as the male's 'throat to breast scarlet with obvious yellow streaks, metallic violet or blue malar streak.' Option E is correct as both sexes have 'heavy, strongly curved bill' and the male's bill is described as 'blackish, dark brown below,' with female 'bare parts as male.'

options.A: The male has a metallic blue-green forehead and crown, with a metallic violet or blue cheek spot.
options.B: The female has a greyish-olive crown, nape, and mantle, with an olive back that brightens to olive-yellow on the rump.
options.C: The male's throat to breast is scarlet with obvious yellow streaks and a metallic violet or blue malar streak.
options.D: The female's underparts are entirely dull orange-scarlet from chin to breast.
options.E: Both sexes have a heavy, strongly curved bill that is blackish or dark brown.

question: Based on the provided monograph, which of the following statements accurately describe the nesting behavior or nest characteristics of Malimbus ibadanensis? Select ALL correct options.

exact_quote: The [the bird] is a solitary nester. It constructs a distinctive hanging-sock-shaped nest primarily in medium to large trees at heights of 15–20 m, sometimes placing the nest near or even adjacent to wasp or hornet nests. The nest has been described as an 'inverted sock' with a globular, lined egg chamber, and a distinctive entrance tube hanging down from the side of the chamber. The entrance tube is approximately 30 cm long. Nests are primarily constructed from shreds of oil-palm fronds and occasionally include tendrils from climbers like Paullinia pinnata.
provenance.reasoning_chain: Options A, B, C, and D are directly supported by the exact quote. Option A is correct because the nest is described as a hanging-sock shape with a globular egg chamber and entrance tube. Option B is correct as nests are placed 15–20 m high in medium to large trees. Option C is correct as nests are sometimes placed near wasp or hornet nests. Option D is correct as construction materials include oil-palm fronds and climber tendrils. Option E is incorrect because the text states the species nests in various habitats including gardens and farmlands, not exclusively in isolated forest interiors, and it tolerates human disturbance.

options.A: It constructs a hanging-sock-shaped nest with a globular egg chamber and a long entrance tube.
options.B: Nests are typically placed 15–20 m high in medium to large native trees.
options.C: Nests are often built near or adjacent to wasp or hornet nests, potentially as a predator-deterrent strategy.
options.D: The nest is primarily constructed from shreds of oil-palm fronds and occasionally includes tendrils from climbers.
options.E: Nests are always built in isolated forest interiors away from any human disturbance.

question: Based on the provided monograph, which of the following statements accurately describe the distribution and population status of Chloropsis flavipennis?

exact_quote: Found only in central and southern Philippines on Leyte, Mindanao, and Samar. Most recent records are from two localities in Mindanao: Bislig (uncommon) and Lake Sebu. It also inhabits portions of the Busa Mountain Range within Mindanao. Previously found on Cebu, where it is now thought to be extirpated as the last known records are from 1920. The status of populations on Leyte and Samar are unknown, as the last known sightings are from 1973 and 1964, respectively.
provenance.reasoning_chain: Option A is correct: the text explicitly states it is found on Leyte, Mindanao, and Samar. Option B is correct: it confirms extirpation from Cebu with last records in 1920. Option D is correct: it mentions the Busa Mountain Range and Lake Sebu in Mindanao as current locations. Option C is incorrect: the text says the status on Leyte and Samar is unknown, with last sightings in 1973 and 1964, not stable with recent sightings. Option E is incorrect: the text states it does not overlap with Yellow-throated Leafbird, which is on Palawan, and [the bird] is not recorded there.

options.A: It is currently found on the islands of Leyte, Mindanao, and Samar.
options.B: It has been extirpated from the island of Cebu, with the last records dating back to 1920.
options.C: Populations on Leyte and Samar are considered stable, with recent sightings in the 2020s.
options.D: It is found in the Busa Mountain Range and Lake Sebu regions of Mindanao.
options.E: It has been recorded on the western island of Palawan, overlapping with the Yellow-throated Leafbird.

question: Based on the provided monograph, which of the following descriptions accurately characterize the appearance of Ploceus hypoxanthus? Select all that apply.

exact_quote: Male nominate race breeding has forehead, crown and nape golden-yellow, mantle, scapulars and back black with greenish-yellow feather fringes, rump yellow; upperwing and tail dark brown, remiges with narrow yellow fringes, wing-coverts with broad pale edges; lores to ear-coverts and to chin and throat black, black extending in a bib onto breast; breast orange-yellow, belly, flanks, thighs and undertail-coverts yellow; iris brown; bill black; legs dull pinkish. options.D: The juvenile is described as resembling the female in plumage.
options.E: Both sexes have bright red legs and a blue bill throughout the year.

question: Based on the provided monograph, which of the following are identified as threats or factors contributing to the decline of Stagonopleura guttata?

exact_quote: Main problems are loss of habitat, remaining fragments of which gradually becoming unsuitable owing to competition with invasive species, overgrazing (which alters vegetation structure), weed invasion, and predation (of adults or young). In New South Wales, despite legislation against large-scale clearing of habitat, approval was given for clearance of 640,000 ha between 1998 and 2005; although not all of this will have been cleared, some was certainly cleared illegally. Principal factors thought to be having adverse impact on this species include loss of important foodplants and habitat through invasion by exotic grasses more suitable for Neochmia temporalis; expansion of latter (which forages in flock) in some areas may have disadvantaged present species. In N of range, changes in fire and grazing regimes thought to have had a major role in the decline. In addition, isolated subpopulations may be susceptible to illegal trapping.
provenance.reasoning_chain: Option A is correct because the text explicitly mentions 'loss of habitat' and 'large-scale clearing of habitat' with illegal clearance. Option B is correct as it cites 'competition with invasive species' and 'overgrazing'. Option C is correct due to 'isolated subpopulations may be susceptible to illegal trapping'. Option E is correct as 'changes in fire and grazing regimes' are noted in the north. Option D is incorrect because while 'predation' is mentioned, it is not specified as being by 'introduced mammalian predators'—the text only states 'predation (of adults or young)' without detailing the predator type, making this a plausible but unconfirmed distractor.

options.A: Loss of habitat through large-scale clearing and fragmentation
options.B: Competition with invasive plant species and overgrazing
options.C: Illegal trapping of isolated subpopulations
options.D: Predation by introduced mammalian predators
options.E: Changes in fire and grazing regimes in northern parts of its range

question: Based on the provided text, which of the following statements accurately describe the distribution or introduction history of Padda oryzivora? Select ALL correct descriptions.

exact_quote: Introduction The [the bird] is thought to be endemic only to Java, Bali, Kangean, and possibly Bawean. A popular cage bird, it has been widely introduced (both intentionally and unintentionally) to many parts of the world. Introductions to China date to the Ming period. In Japan, the [the bird] is mentioned in a handbook of Japanese foods and in a dictionary of the Japanese language published in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, respectively. In the past, this species was released in Taiwan during religious ceremonies as an offering to the dead. Early attempts at introducing [the bird]s to North America and the Hawaiian Is. during the latter half of the nineteenth century were unsuccessful. Sightings were first documented in Florida in the mid-1950s and on O‘ahu I., Hawaiian Archipelago, in 1964. In Florida, this species reached a peak in numbers in 1969 but was extirpated during the following decade. In contrast, the population on O‘ahu I. has undergone explosive growth: from 4 birds documented on the Honolulu Christmas Bird Count (CBC) in 1969 to 1,096 tallied on this same count in 1995. In addition, [the bird]s have expanded their distribution to the islands of Hawai‘i, Kaua‘i, Maui, and Moloka‘i. On Puerto Rico, it is established in the capital of San Juan.
provenance.reasoning_chain: Option A is correct as the text states '[the bird] is thought to be endemic only to Java, Bali, Kangean, and possibly Bawean.' Option B is incorrect because while the bird was introduced to Florida and peaked in numbers in 1969, it was 'extirpated during the following decade' and did not establish a permanent population. Option C is correct as the text explicitly mentions expansion to 'the islands of Hawai‘i, Kaua‘i, Maui, and Moloka‘i' after initial establishment on O‘ahu. Option D is correct because 'Introductions to China date to the Ming period' and later text in the Distribution chapter notes successful introduction in parts of eastern China. Option E is incorrect as the text states unsuccessful introductions to New Zealand and Australia, with no mention of establishment or common status there.

options.A: It is endemic only to Java, Bali, Kangean, and possibly Bawean.
options.B: It was successfully introduced to Florida and established a permanent population there.
options.C: It has been introduced to the Hawaiian Islands and is now found on multiple islands including O‘ahu, Hawai‘i, Kaua‘i, Maui, and Moloka‘i.
options.D: It was introduced to China during the Ming period and is established in parts of eastern China.
options.E: It has been successfully introduced to Australia and New Zealand, where it remains common.

question: Based on the provided monograph, which of the following behaviors are correctly described for Amandava formosa? Select ALL correct answers.

exact_quote: Forages mostly on ground. Gregarious; occurs in flocks in non-breeding season, sometimes mixing with A. [the bird]. Therefore, estimated population size suspected to fall in the range of 1000–2500 mature individuals with no subpopulation comprising more than 250 mature individuals BirdLife International (2018) Species factsheet: [the bird]. question: Based on the provided text, which of the following statements accurately describe morphological differences between Passer zarudnyi and its formerly conspecific relative P. simplex?

exact_quote: Compared to formerly conspecific P. simplex has has shorter wing and bill, and longer tail. Female is similar to male in plumage but with grey often slightly tinged buff, and black on head (not extending behind eye) and bib reduced and browner, and is thus obviously quite different from same-sex P. simplex, by also having the entire ventral plumage off-white to grey-white, with some very slight buffish elements (in female P. simplex the underparts are white with bright or deep buffish elements of variable extent but always far more extensive and noticeable), the upperparts are principally pale grey, albeit with some pale buffy elements on the back, scapulars and rump (the upperparts of P. simplex are buffy ochre and the latter species almost never shows any trace of dark bases to the greater coverts) and the bill is seemingly always all black (like males) at least when nesting. Juvenile resembles female.

question: Based on the monograph, which of the following statements accurately describe the vocal behavior of Vidua paradisaea?

exact_quote: Male mimics calls and songs of host species, the Melba Finch; songs vary in elements and sequence, vary also regionally much as do those of its host. Males match songs of local populations and races of Melba Finch, which differ among regions (e.g. S Somalia and NE Kenya; Paré Mts, in NE Tanzania; and Lochinvar National Park, in Zambia). Males at L Baringo, in Kenya, mimics songs and calls of Blue-capped Cordon-bleu (Uraeginthus cyanocephalus), perhaps indicative of a brood-parasitic relationship; this whydah's distribution in Ethiopia matches that of Blue-capped Cordon-bleu in regions where Melba Finch does not occur. In addition, male gives non-mimetic calls, high and thin, sweet and hissing, 'weeeee', 'weee-tssss' or 'seeee-tsi-tseeeew', triple hissing 'sss-sss-ssssss', buzzier 'zzzeeee', sometimes in mix of chatters and short notes. Both sexes give non-mimetic chatters, the calls soft in flight, long and rapid when perched, and loud and complex before flying. Begging call of nestling initially like that of nestling Melba Finch; later becomes more distinct, a husky, harsh 'chew chew chew' (Melba Finch 'chuc chuc, peett').

Option D is correct as males at Lake Baringo mimic Blue-capped Cordon-bleu, suggesting a possible brood-parasitic relationship. Option E is correct as nestling begging calls initially resemble Melba Finch but later become distinct 'chew chew chew'.
